title: Jeremiah 26:1–16
context: The narrator dates this word to the beginning of Jehoiakim’s reign, and the LORD commands Jeremiah to stand in the court of the LORD’s house and speak every word, “It may be they will listen,” warning that otherwise “I will make this house like Shiloh.” The priests, the prophets, and all the people seize Jeremiah, saying, “You shall surely die!” and when the princes come, Jeremiah answers that the LORD sent him, calls the people to amend their ways so that “the LORD will relent,” and places himself in their hands, until the princes and the people declare, “This man is not worthy of death.” Many readers connect this scene with the temple sermon of 7:1–15, which is named here without harmonizing the two accounts, and the relenting language points to the existing boxes at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10 rather than a new one, while both traditions share the ground that God’s warnings are sincere calls to repentance.

verses.text: In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the LORD:
verses.arminianNotes:
“In the beginning of the reign of Jehoiakim the son of Josiah, king of Judah, this word came from the LORD.” Arminian readers note that this places the scene earlier than chapter 25’s fourth year.

The book is not arranged in strict chronological order.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise note the arrangement and do not force a sequence on it.

Shared ground: both traditions read the date as setting the trial early in Jehoiakim’s reign, and both name 7:1–15 as a related account without harmonizing the details.

verses.text: “The LORD says: ‘Stand in the court of the LORD’s house, and speak to all the cities of Judah which come to worship in the LORD’s house, all the words that I command you to speak to them. Don’t omit a word.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “Stand in the court of the LORD’s house, and speak to all the cities of Judah which come to worship in the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note the public setting before worshipers.

The command “Don’t omit a word” stresses faithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet’s duty to speak the whole word, however unwelcome.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that faithful ministry declares the full message entrusted to it, and that Jeremiah is commanded not to soften it.

verses.text: It may be they will listen, and every man turn from his evil way, that I may relent from the evil which I intend to do to them because of the evil of their doings.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says, “It may be they will listen, and every man turn from his evil way, that I may relent from the evil which I intend to do to them.” Arminian readers take this as God’s real responsiveness to repentance.

They point to the existing boxes at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers read the relenting within God’s unchanging purpose, which includes repentance as its means, pointing to the same boxes.

Shared ground: both traditions agree the offer is sincere, that “evil” here means disaster, and that God delights in repentance (cf. 18:7–8).

verses.text: You shall tell them, “The LORD says: ‘If you will not listen to me, to walk in my law which I have set before you,
verses.arminianNotes:
“If you will not listen to me, to walk in my law which I have set before you.” Arminian readers note the conditional form of the warning.

The law is described as set before them, a gift as well as a demand.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the covenant’s terms laid before the people.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the warning is conditional in form and that the people are responsible to hear and obey the LORD’s law.

verses.text: to listen to the words of my servants the prophets whom I send to you, even rising up early and sending them—but you have not listened—
verses.arminianNotes:
The people were “to listen to the words of my servants the prophets whom I send to you, even rising up early and sending them.” Arminian readers note the LORD’s persistent sending of prophets (cf. 25:4).

The interruption “but you have not listened” names the problem.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God’s faithful and repeated warnings.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the prophets were God’s gracious provision and that rejecting them was rejecting the LORD himself.

verses.text: then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD warns, “then I will make this house like Shiloh, and will make this city a curse to all the nations of the earth.” Arminian readers note the reference to Shiloh, where the sanctuary once stood (cf. 7:12–14).

The temple’s presence did not guarantee safety.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a warning against trusting in religious institutions apart from obedience.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that God’s presence is not bound to a building in a way that excuses sin, and they name 7:12–14 without harmonizing.

verses.text: The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The priests and the prophets and all the people heard Jeremiah speaking these words in the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note the audience that will soon become his accusers.

The religious leaders are present.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the setting prepared for the conflict that follows.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the narrator’s transition, naming the groups who hear Jeremiah’s message.

verses.text: When Jeremiah had finished speaking all that the LORD had commanded him to speak to all the people, the priests and the prophets and all the people seized him, saying, “You shall surely die!
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests, the prophets, and all the people seized Jeremiah, saying, “You shall surely die!” Arminian readers note the violent reaction to the message.

The priests and prophets lead the response.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the hostility that faithful preaching can provoke.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that Jeremiah’s suffering for the word is part of the prophetic pattern, and both read the scene soberly.

verses.text: Why have you prophesied in the LORD’s name, saying, ‘This house will be like Shiloh, and this city will be desolate, without inhabitant’?” All the people were crowded around Jeremiah in the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
The accusers ask why Jeremiah has prophesied in the LORD’s name that “This house will be like Shiloh.” Arminian readers note that the charge is the content of the prophecy itself.

They see it as an attack on the temple.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the accusers unable to accept a word of judgment against the temple.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that the people’s confidence in the temple, criticized in 7:4, made the message seem like blasphemy to them.

verses.text: When the princes of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king’s house to the LORD’s house; and they sat in the entry of the new gate of the LORD’s house.
verses.arminianNotes:
“When the princes of Judah heard these things, they came up from the king’s house to the LORD’s house.” Arminian readers note that civil officials arrive to hear the case.

They sit “in the entry of the new gate,” a place of judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see a legal setting forming.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as introducing the princes as judges, which leads to a more measured hearing than the crowd’s first reaction.

verses.text: Then the priests and the prophets spoke to the princes and to all the people, saying, “This man is worthy of death, for he has prophesied against this city, as you have heard with your ears.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The priests and prophets say, “This man is worthy of death, for he has prophesied against this city.” Arminian readers note that they formally accuse Jeremiah before the princes.

Their charge rests on the content of the message.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the religious leaders opposing the prophet.

Shared ground: both traditions note that the accusers are the priests and prophets, and both read the scene as a warning that religious office does not guarantee faithfulness.

verses.text: Then Jeremiah spoke to all the princes and to all the people, saying, “The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that you have heard.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah answers, “The LORD sent me to prophesy against this house and against this city all the words that you have heard.” Arminian readers note that his defense is his commission.

He does not retract the message.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet resting on God’s call.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that Jeremiah’s courage comes from his confidence that the word is the LORD’s, not his own.

verses.text: Now therefore amend your ways and your doings, and obey the LORD your God’s voice; then the LORD will relent from the evil that he has pronounced against you.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah says, “Now therefore amend your ways and your doings, and obey the LORD your God’s voice; then the LORD will relent from the evil that he has pronounced against you.” Arminian readers see a real offer.

They point to the existing boxes at 1 Samuel 15:29 and Jonah 3:10.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise affirm the offer’s sincerity and read the relenting within God’s unchanging purpose, pointing to the same boxes.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that even on trial Jeremiah calls his accusers to repent.

verses.text: But as for me, behold, I am in your hand. Do with me what is good and right in your eyes.
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah says, “But as for me, behold, I am in your hand. Do with me what is good and right in your eyes.” Arminian readers note his submission to the court.

He does not resist or flee.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet trusting God while accepting human authority.

Shared ground: both traditions read his words as courage joined to humility, an example for those who suffer for faithful witness.

verses.text: Only know for certain that if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood on yourselves, on this city, and on its inhabitants; for in truth the LORD has sent me to you to speak all these words in your ears.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Jeremiah warns, “if you put me to death, you will bring innocent blood on yourselves, on this city, and on its inhabitants.” Arminian readers note the seriousness of shedding innocent blood.

He insists “in truth the LORD has sent me.”
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see the prophet warning his judges of their accountability before God.

Shared ground: both traditions agree that harming God’s messengers is grave sin, and that Jeremiah speaks out of conviction rather than self-defense alone.

verses.text: Then the princes and all the people said to the priests and to the prophets: “This man is not worthy of death; for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God.”
verses.arminianNotes:
The princes and all the people say, “This man is not worthy of death; for he has spoken to us in the name of the LORD our God.” Arminian readers note that the people’s view has shifted.

The princes judge more fairly than the priests and prophets.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise see God protecting his servant through the civil leaders.

Shared ground: both traditions read the verdict as a moment of justice in a hostile setting, without overstating the people’s repentance.
